en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk 19.
The Training Rule on Trading in Silver:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks engaged in various kinds of transactions involving money.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, engage in various kinds of transactions involving money, just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures?"
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and resenting.
Those monks who were few in desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and resented, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks engage in various kinds of transactions involving money?"
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
[The Buddha said: “… Is it true, monks, that you engaged in various kinds of transactions involving money?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“…How can you, foolish men, engage in various kinds of transactions involving money?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so forth].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, however, a monk should engage in various kinds of transactions involving money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
“Whosoever, however,” means:
Whoever such as this … [as above] … is called a “bhikkhu” … [as above] …; this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Of various kinds" means that which is done,
that which is not done, and that which is both done and not done.
"Done" means...
[It may be] reaching the head, reaching the neck, reaching the hands, reaching the feet, or reaching the waist.
What is called "made" refers to what has been thoroughly made.
"Made and unmade" refers to both of those.
"Silver" means:
A coin the color of the Teacher, a copper māsaka, a wooden māsaka, or a lacquer māsaka—these are what enter into commerce.
"Should she obtain" means:
if she causes something already made to be exchanged for another thing already made, it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense.
If one causes what has been made to be exchanged for what has not been made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one causes what has been made to be exchanged for what has been both made and not made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one causes what has not been made to be exchanged for what has been made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one exchanges what has not been made for what has not been made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one exchanges what has not been made for what has been both made and not made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one exchanges what has been both made and not made for what has been made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If she exchanges what has been made and not made for what has not been made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. If she exchanges what has been made and not made for what has been made and not made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
It must be forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:

That monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
"Venerable sirs, I engaged in various kinds of transactions involving money."
“This is my article to be relinquished. I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
Having relinquished it, the offense should be confessed.
An offense should be received by a competent monk who is capable.
If a monastery attendant or a lay follower arrives there, he should be told:
"Friend, please take note of this."
If he says, "What should be brought by this [person]?",
one should not say:
“Bring this or that. One should point out what is allowable:
ghee, oil, honey, or molasses.
If he exchanges it for that and brings back something allowable, then—with the exception of the one who handled the money—all may use it.
If it can be obtained in this way, that is good;
if it cannot be obtained, he should be told:
“Friend, discard this.
If he discards it, that is well.
If he does not discard it, a monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the discarder of money:

One who would not go astray through desire, nor go astray through hatred, nor go astray through delusion, nor go astray through fear, and who can distinguish between what has been discarded and what has not been discarded—
“And furthermore, monks, he is to be appointed in this way:
first, a monk is to be requested.”
Having made the request, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money.”
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me.
The Sangha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of silver.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of silver, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the discarder of silver.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent;
thus do I hold this.
That appointed monk, having made a mark, should drop [the bowl].
If he causes it to fall after making a sign, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, regarding money as money, he exchanges money for [goods], there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If, regarding money with doubt, he exchanges money for [goods], there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one perceives what is not money as money and exchanges it for money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If one perceives what is money as not money and exchanges it for money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one is in doubt regarding what is not money and exchanges it for money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one exchanges non-monetary goods for monetary goods while perceiving them as non-monetary, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one exchanges non-monetary goods for monetary goods while perceiving them as monetary, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one exchanges non-monetary goods for monetary goods while being in doubt, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is formless and he perceives it as formless, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender":
thus ends the ninth training rule concerning trading in money.
